question: An events team wants to put a Claude-drafted safety briefing for a public open day on the venue website tomorrow. Nobody has yet been named to check it. What should the team lead do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to review its own briefing and confirm that the safety guidance in it is accurate.
B) Decide who has to sign the briefing off, given that it is public and safety-related content.
C) Publish the briefing and ask staff on the day to correct anything that turns out to be wrong.
D) Circulate the briefing to the whole team so that anyone who wishes to can comment on it.
correct_answers: B) Decide who has to sign the briefing off, given that it is public and safety-related content.
explanations: Asking the same conversation to certify its own accuracy provides reassurance rather than assurance, and it does not put a person's name against the content.

Correct. Public, safety-related content sits at the top of the range where a named human must review and own the output before it goes out. Establishing who that person is comes before anything else, because it determines whether tomorrow's deadline is even achievable.

Correcting a published safety briefing after members of the public have read it does not undo the harm. High visibility and low reversibility are precisely the conditions that call for review before release, not after.
General circulation invites comment without assigning responsibility. Everyone may assume someone else has checked the safety guidance, which is how an unreviewed briefing reaches the public.
